title: status & log
subtitle: Inspect your repo state and history
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: After working for an hour, you need to know: what files did I change? What did I commit? Did I already stage that fix? Without inspection commands, you're flying blind.
whyItExists.solution: git status shows the current state of your working tree and staging area. git log shows the commit history. git diff shows exactly what changed line by line.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Before every commit (git status). Before pushing (git log). When reviewing what changed (git diff). Constantly.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: These are read-only commands — safe to run anytime.

explainModes.beginner: git status tells you what's changed and what's staged. git log shows the list of commits like a timeline. git diff shows the actual lines that changed — additions in green, deletions in red.
explainModes.simple: git status — shows modified, staged, and untracked files. git log --oneline -- compact history. git diff -- working tree vs staging. git diff --staged -- staging vs last commit. git show <hash> -- shows a specific commit.
explainModes.standard: git status --short (-s) shows a compact two-column format: left column = staging area, right = working tree. git log has powerful formatting: --graph (branch diagram), --all (all branches), --author, --since, --grep. git log -p shows the diff for each commit. git diff HEAD compares working tree to last commit.
explainModes.technical: git log follows the parent chain from HEAD backward. The reflog (git reflog) records every change to HEAD, including resets and rebases — a safety net for recovering deleted commits. git bisect uses binary search over the commit history to find which commit introduced a bug. git blame <file> shows the last commit for every line of a file.
explainModes.deepDive: git log --format accepts printf-style format strings: %H (full hash), %h (short), %an (author name), %ae (author email), %s (subject), %cd (commit date). Git notes (git notes) attach metadata to commits without changing their hash. Git's diff algorithm can be configured: myers (default), histogram (better for code), patience (better for long files). git log --follow tracks a file across renames.

content.code:
$ git status
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   src/index.html        ← STAGED

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
        modified:   src/style.css         ← MODIFIED

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        src/new-page.html                 ← NEW

# Short format — compact view
$ git status -s
M  src/index.html   ← staged (green M)
 M src/style.css    ← unstaged (red M)
?? src/new-page.html  ← untracked

# Full log
git log

# Compact one-line per commit
git log --oneline
# a3f2c1d (HEAD -> main) Add dark mode toggle
# 8b9e4f2 Fix login button on mobile
# 2c1a5e8 Add user profile page

# With branch graph (great for visualising merges)
git log --oneline --graph --all

# Filter by author
git log --author="Prashant"

# Filter by date
git log --since="2 weeks ago"
git log --after="2026-09-01"

# Search commit messages
git log --grep="fix"

# Show what changed in each commit (patches)
git log -p

# Unstaged changes (working tree vs staging area)
git diff

# Staged changes (staging area vs last commit)
git diff --staged

# All changes (working tree vs last commit)
git diff HEAD

# Compare two commits
git diff a3f2c1d 8b9e4f2

# See what a specific commit changed
git show a3f2c1d

# See diff for one file only
git diff HEAD -- src/index.html

questions.question: What does git log --oneline show?
options: All commits, one per line with short hash and message
questions.explanation: --oneline shows all commits in the current branch's history, one per line: short hash + commit message. Add --all to include all branches.

faq.q: How do I search for a commit that introduced a bug?
faq.a: Use git bisect — it binary-searches your history to find the bad commit. Start with git bisect start, mark the current commit as bad with git bisect bad, mark a known-good commit with git bisect good <hash>, then Git checks out the midpoint for you to test.

faq.q: How do I see who last changed a line?
faq.a: git blame <filename> shows each line with the commit hash, author, and date of the last change. In VS Code, the GitLens extension shows blame inline while you code.
